terms.meaning: Young folded mountains, like the Himalayas, from Alaska to Panama; the Rockies are the main range.
The vast, treeless Great Central Plains, called the "Wheat bowl" of the world.
Very old rocks around Hudson Bay, like the Deccan Plateau.
The belt of evergreen coniferous forest south of the Tundra: pine, fir, spruce.
A region specialising in one crop, such as the Corn belt or Cotton belt.
A person who cuts timber in Canada.

items.name: Location of North America
items.formula: Entirely north of the equator, 7°N to 84°N; the Bering Strait separates it from Asia.
items.example: The Isthmus of Panama links it to South America.

items.name: Size of North America
items.formula: Third largest continent, after Asia and Africa: 24.24 million sq km, about 7 times India.
items.example: 24 countries; the largest are Canada, USA and Mexico. Greenland is its largest island.

items.name: Four physical divisions of North America
items.formula: Western Cordilleras (Rockies), Great Central Plains, Canadian Shield, Appalachian Highlands.
items.example: Compare: Rockies like the Himalayas, Shield like the Deccan.

items.name: Highest and lowest points
items.formula: Mount McKinley (6194 m) is the highest; Death Valley (86 m below sea level) the lowest.
items.example: Plateaus between the ranges: Columbia, Colorado, Mexican.

items.name: Grand Canyon and Old Faithful
items.formula: The Colorado river cut the Grand Canyon (about 1800 m deep, 3 to 29 km wide).
items.example: Old Faithful is a geyser in Yellowstone National Park.

items.name: Appalachian Highlands
items.formula: Old folded mountains worn down, from Newfoundland to Alabama.
items.example: Rich in coal, lead, zinc and iron; the St. Lawrence valley separates them from the Labrador plateau.

items.name: Rivers of North America
items.formula: Mississippi and Missouri drain 2/3 of the land; the Mississippi flows into the Gulf of Mexico.
items.example: The St. Lawrence passes the Great Lakes and is frozen 3 months a year.

items.name: The Great Lakes (HOMES)
items.formula: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie and Superior.
items.example: Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world; Chicago is on Lake Michigan.

items.name: Tundra
items.formula: Inside the Arctic Circle: mosses and lichens; reindeer, caribou and polar bears.
items.example: Found in Canada, Alaska and Greenland.

items.name: Other forest belts
items.formula: Deciduous (oak, chestnut) east of the Great Lakes; tropical (mahogany) in Mexico and the West Indies.
items.example: California has a Mediterranean climate; the south-west has cactus deserts.

items.name: Farming in North America
items.formula: Only ten percent of the land is farmed, but output is huge: wheat in the Prairies, maize in USA and Mexico.
items.example: Cuba is the "Sugar bowl of the world"; California is the "Wine Country".

items.name: Minerals of North America
items.formula: Gold in California; iron around Lake Superior; Mexico leads in silver; USA leads in copper.
items.example: Appalachian coal; USA is the largest coal exporter.

items.name: Industries of North America
items.formula: Pittsburgh is the "Steel city"; Chicago is known for plastics and meat packing.
items.example: Canada is a top exporter of paper, pulp and newsprint.

items.name: People of North America
items.formula: Mostly Europeans, American Indians and Africans, speaking English, Spanish or French.
items.example: About 98% live in towns; the east is most crowded, the icy north almost empty.

mistakes.text: North America is the third largest continent; Asia and Africa are bigger.
Lake Superior, not Michigan, is the largest of the Great Lakes.
The Rockies are young folded mountains in the west; the Appalachians are old, worn-down mountains in the east.
